indexes {
    (id, country) [pk] // composite primary key
    created_at [name: 'created_at_index', note: 'Date']
    booking_date
    (country, booking_date) [unique]
    booking_date [type: hash]
    (`id*2`)
    (`id*3`,`getdate()`)
    (`id*3`,id)
  }

type of the data in the column listed as `column_type`
  - supports all data types. The type name must not contain spaces; if your type has a space (e.g. `double precision`), wrap it in double quotes: `"double precision"`. Types with parentheses like `decimal(1,2)` or `varchar(255)` are supported as-is

Each operator can be augmented with `?` on either side to make that side **optional** — meaning the FK column is nullable and rows don't have to match.

For example, `>?` means the referenced side is optional, `?>` means the source side is optional. This works with all operators.

- `<`: one-to-many. E.g: `users.id < posts.user_id`
- `>`: many-to-one. E.g: `posts.user_id > users.id`
- `-`: one-to-one. E.g: `users.id - user_infos.user_id`
- `<>`: many-to-many. E.g: `authors.id <> books.id`

raw_evidence.quote: A new schema will be defined as long as it contains any table or enum. ... By default, any **table**, **relationship**, or **enum** definition that omits `schema_name` will be considered to belong to the `public` schema.

`DiagramView` allows users to define multiple views of a database diagram, each focusing on different tables, notes, table groups, or schemas.

Each view can include one or more of the following categories:

- `Tables`: specific tables to include
- `Notes`: specific sticky notes to include
- `TableGroups`: specific table groups to include
- `Schemas`: specific schemas to include

Use `{ * }` to include all items in a category, or specify a line-separated list of names

`TableGroup` allows users to group the related or associated tables together.

TableGroup tablegroup_name { // tablegroup is case-insensitive.
  table1
  table2
  table3
}
`null` or `not null`: mark a column null or not null. If you omit this setting, the column will be null by default

composite_primary_keys.citation: docs.md 'Index Definition' section — `(id, country) [pk]` inside a table's `indexes { }` block
composite_primary_keys.rationale: The Index Definition section explicitly documents wrapping two or more column names in parentheses with a `[pk]` setting as the mechanism for a composite primary key; the same mechanism composes for OUTCOME_RULE, NAMED_RESOURCE_LINK, and CONDITION_POST.

json_payload_columns.citation: docs.md 'Table Definition' section — column_type 'supports all data types'
json_payload_columns.rationale: DBML column types are free-form strings passed through to the target dialect (e.g. `json` or `jsonb` for Postgres); no restriction on type name beyond the space-quoting rule, so an opaque JSON payload column is a plain native column type, not a workaround.

enumerated_string_domains.rationale: `enum name { value1 value2 ... }` plus referencing the enum name as a column type is a first-class, dedicated language construct for exactly this case.

several_self_referencing_foreign_keys_on.citation: docs.md 'Relationships & Foreign Key Definitions' section (general Ref syntax, table.column > table.column, no same-table restriction stated); corroborated by a parser test fixture, see source-dbml-contrary-evidence.json
several_self_referencing_foreign_keys_on.rationale: The Ref/relationship grammar names a source and target as schema.table.column pairs with no rule barring the same table on both sides, and each Ref statement is independent, so multiple self-referencing Refs on one table compose. Docs.md itself contains no worked example with three simultaneous self-refs on one table — this classification also rests on the parser test fixture cited in source-dbml-contrary-evidence.json, which shows two independent self-referencing Refs on two different tables (not three on one), so the 'three at once' scaling is inferred from the absence of a stated limit, not directly demonstrated.

nullable_foreign_keys.citation: docs.md 'Column Settings' (`null`/`not null`, default null) and 'Relationships & Foreign Key Definitions' (`?` optional-side modifier)
nullable_foreign_keys.rationale: A referencing column is nullable by default unless marked `not null`; the relationship operator can additionally be suffixed with `?` to mark a side optional, giving two independent, directly documented mechanisms.

multi_column_unique_constraints.rationale: The same indexes{} block used for composite PKs supports a `[unique]` setting on a parenthesized multi-column tuple, independent of any `[pk]` setting.

one_to_zero_or_one_relationships.citation: docs.md 'Relationships & Foreign Key Definitions' — one-to-one operator `-` combined with the `?` optional-side modifier ('This works with all operators')
one_to_zero_or_one_relationships.rationale: The docs state the optional-side `?` modifier applies to all four relationship operators including `-` (one-to-one); applying `?` to the referencing side of a one-to-one Ref yields exactly a one-to-zero-or-one relationship. No worked example shows `-?` specifically (only `>?` is shown), so this is a direct rule application rather than a copied example.

value_constraint_beyond_type.citation: docs.md 'Check Definition' section — `checks { ... }` block and column-level `check:` setting
value_constraint_beyond_type.rationale: DBML has a dedicated construct for arbitrary check expressions ('otherwise impossible to express'). It is a native language feature, not a workaround at the DBML level; however the expression itself is opaque backtick-quoted text that DBML does not parse or validate, so the actual disjunction (decimal positive integer OR literal 'ALL') must be phrased as valid SQL for the target dialect — DBML supplies the slot, not the semantics.

several_logical_schemas_one_database.rationale: Any table, enum, or relationship can be prefixed with an arbitrary schema_name (`Table core.users { }`, `Table blogging.posts { }`); tables/relationships/enums without a prefix default to `public`. Nothing limits the number of distinct schema_name values in one file, so configuration/runtime/audit/resources map directly to four schema_name prefixes.

named_subset_views_over_one_model.rationale: DiagramView is a first-class, named construct that selects a filtered subset of Tables, Notes, TableGroups, or Schemas for one view, directly analogous to Structurizr's views. It is documented but not dated to a specific release in the changelog, and (see source-dbml-contrary-evidence.json) the open-source third-party CLI renderer (dbml-renderer) shows no code reference to DiagramView, so whether the containerizable rendering path actually restricts output to one DiagramView is unconfirmed by primary source — only that the language construct exists and is parsed by @dbml/core/@dbml/parse.

contrary_evidence_search.result: No documentation or issue stating that composite PKs, enums, multi-column unique, nullable FKs, or check expressions are unsupported. No explicit statement either confirming or denying that three simultaneous self-referencing FKs on one table are supported — grammar and a two-table test fixture (not a three-FK single-table case) are the closest primary evidence. No changelog entry pinpointing DiagramView's introduction date was found, and no evidence that any open-source renderer currently honours a DiagramView filter when producing SVG/PNG output — this is recorded as an unresolved gap, not a confirmed capability of the rendering toolchain.
